newsitem.title: USA: U.S. may enhance troop protection in Gulf - Cohen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may enhance troop protection in Gulf - Cohen.

text.p: The United States may take additional protective measures for U.S. forces in the Gulf based on a White House report questioning security at some military and diplomatic posts in the area, Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Thursday.

"Anytime that anyone makes an assessment that we are in any way deficient, we take it very seriously," Cohen told reporters of the recent study by a National Security Council expert regarding safety from terrorist attack in the Gulf.

"We will look at the Simon report very carefully and take whatever additional measures need to be taken," the secretary added during a Pentagon photo opportunity with visiting Malaysian Defence Minister Syed Hamid Albar.
The recent memo by NSC official Steve Simon to the White House follows two car bombings in Saudi Arabia, one last June and the other in 1995, that killed a total of 24 U.S. troops.

Cohen was not specific on what new measures might be taken, but Washington has already made costly Gulf security moves, including the movement of more than 6,000 U.S. Air Force personnel in Saudi Arabia to a remote air base and other protected facilities in the kingdom.

The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Simon wrote after a recent visit to the region that there were gaps in security at several facilities, including an air base in Kuwait where U.S. crews are stationed, an apartment building in Bahrain that houses American naval personnel, a port in the United Arab Emirates where U.S. aircraft carriers dock and an American Embassy in the region.

"I'm familiar with the report that was filed with the NSC and others. We take it very seriously," said Cohen. He noted that Deputy U.S. Defence Secretary John White was currently in the Gulf region on a long-planned visit and was studying security.
But Cohen was cautious in the wake of the bombing last June 25 at a military housing complex in Dhahran that killed 25 U.S. servicemen.
"I should point out that we can never provide 100 percent full protection for our forces who are dispersed throughout the world," he said.
"We will take whatever measures are necessary to provide the best possible guarantee against terrorist attacks against our forces, but there can be no 100 percent, fool-proof guarantee."

Although Saudi Arabia executed several men blamed for the November 1995 bombing in Riyadh that killed five U.S. troops, there has been no final assessment of blame for last year's bombing at Khobar Towers military housing complex in Dhahran.

A Pentagon report issued last year was scathing in putting some responsibility for the explosion on senior U.S. officers on the scene and at the Pentagon, saying that not enough had been done to protect American troops from attack.

The U.S. Air Force in January delayed the promotion of Brig. Gen. Terryl Schwalier to major general in a controversy over the Dhahran bombing pending an additional study of the matter ordered by Deputy Defence Secretary White.

Schwalier, who commanded U.S. air operations in Saudi Arabia when the truck bomb ripped the housing complex, was already nominated by President Bill Clinton and confirmed by the Senate for the promotion.
The Air Force has repeatedly insisted that Schwalier and other officers took necessary safety measures ahead of the bombing based on information they had at the time.
